# Project Environments for R and Python {#sec-environments}

## Overview

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="The task: give each project its own packages"}

R and Python packages change between versions, and a new version can change a result.
If every project on your computer shares one set of packages, updating a package for
one project can quietly change another. A **project environment** avoids this. It is a
set of packages that belongs to one project folder, together with a **lockfile**: a
text file that records the exact version of every package.

With an environment and its lockfile, you can come back to an analysis next year, or
hand it to a collaborator, and run it with the same packages.

This chapter covers three tools. You do not need all three.

| Tool | Manages | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) | R packages | Your project uses R. |
| [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | Python and Python packages | Your project uses Python. |
| [pixi](https://pixi.sh/) | Python, R, and other software together | One environment must hold both languages, or software that is neither. |

For each tool, you will learn to **create** an environment, **add** packages to it,
**activate** it, **deactivate** it, and **delete** it, and how Positron and Quarto
find it.

A project with R and Python can simply use renv and uv side by side, each with its own
lockfile. This book does that. We do not use conda.

In this chapter, blocks labelled R go in the **R console** and blocks labelled Bash go
in the **terminal** (see @sec-positron). None of them run when the book is rendered.
Work in a new, empty practice folder opened in Positron, not in the book's folder.

:::

## The five tasks at a glance

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="One table to return to"}

| Task | renv (R console) | uv (terminal) | pixi (terminal) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Create | `renv::init()` | `uv init --bare --python 3.13` | `pixi init` |
| Add a package | `renv::install("dplyr")`, then `renv::snapshot()` | `uv add pandas` | `pixi add pandas` |
| Remove a package | `renv::remove("dplyr")`, then `renv::snapshot()` | `uv remove pandas` | `pixi remove pandas` |
| Activate | Automatic when R starts in the folder | `source .venv/bin/activate`, or prefix commands with `uv run` | `pixi shell`, or prefix commands with `pixi run` |
| Deactivate | `renv::deactivate()` | `deactivate` | `exit` |
| Delete installed packages, keeping the lockfile | Delete `renv/library`, then restart R | Delete the `.venv` folder | `pixi clean` |
| Rebuild from the lockfile | `renv::restore()` | `uv sync --locked` | `pixi install --locked` |
| Lockfile | `renv.lock` | `uv.lock` | `pixi.lock` |

**Activate** means "use this project's packages now". **Deactivate** means "stop using
them"; the environment stays on disk. **Delete** removes the installed packages. As
long as you keep the lockfile, deleting is safe, because the last row rebuilds the
environment.

:::

## renv: R packages

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Create"}

Install renv once per computer, from the R console:

```{.r}
install.packages("renv")
```

Then open your project folder in Positron and create the environment:

```{.r}
renv::init()
```

renv adds three things to the folder and restarts R:

| File or folder | Purpose | Share through Git? |
|---|---|---|
| `renv.lock` | The lockfile: R's version and each package's version. | Yes |
| `.Rprofile` | One line that switches R to the project library when R starts here. | Yes |
| `renv/` | The project library and renv's settings. | Only `activate.R`, `settings.json`, and `.gitignore`; renv hides the library from Git for you. |

`renv::init()` reads your scripts and `.qmd` files and installs the packages they
use. In an empty folder there is nothing to find, so the lockfile starts with renv
alone. To start empty on purpose in a folder that already has code, use
`renv::init(bare = TRUE)`.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Add packages"}

```{.r}
renv::install("dplyr")
```

This installs dplyr into the project library only. The lockfile has not changed yet.
Use the package in your code, for example `dplyr::filter()` in a `.qmd` file, and then
record it:

```{.r}
renv::snapshot()
```

By default, `renv::snapshot()` records the packages your project's files use, and the
packages those depend on. A package you installed but never used is left out. This
keeps the lockfile to what the analysis needs.

To render Quarto documents that contain R chunks, the project library also needs
**knitr** and **rmarkdown**. A new renv environment does not have them, and
`quarto render` stops with "The knitr package is not available" until you add them:

```{.r}
renv::install(c("knitr", "rmarkdown"))
renv::snapshot()
```

Two commands help you keep track:

```{.r}
renv::status()    # Do the library, the lockfile, and your code agree?
renv::remove("dplyr")   # Uninstall a package from the project library.
```

After removing a package, run `renv::snapshot()` again so the lockfile matches.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Activate"}

There is no command to type. When R starts in the project folder, `.Rprofile` runs
and switches R to the project library. In Positron, open the folder and start an R
session. The console confirms it:

```{.default}
- Project '~/projects/my-analysis' loaded. [renv 1.2.2]
```

You can check where R is looking for packages. The first path should be inside your
project's `renv/` folder:

```{.r}
.libPaths()
```

Quarto starts R in the project folder too, so `quarto render` uses the project
library, provided knitr and rmarkdown are installed in it (see "Add packages" above).

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Deactivate"}

```{.r}
renv::deactivate()
```

This removes the line from `.Rprofile` and restarts R, which goes back to your
computer's general package library. `renv.lock` and the `renv/` folder stay where they
are. To switch the project library back on:

```{.r}
renv::activate()
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Delete, and rebuild"}

To remove renv from a project completely:

```{.r}
renv::deactivate(clean = TRUE)
```

This deletes the `renv/` folder **and `renv.lock`**. Your scripts and data are not
touched, but the record of package versions is gone, so use it only when you no longer
want the project to use renv.

More often you want a fresh copy of the same environment, for example after a failed
installation. Delete the library and keep the lockfile: remove the `renv/library`
folder in Positron's file explorer, restart R, and run:

```{.r}
renv::restore()
```

`renv::restore()` is also the command a collaborator runs after downloading your
project. It installs the versions in `renv.lock`.

renv records R's version but does not install R. If the lockfile names a different
version of R from yours, renv tells you. Some recorded packages may not be compatible
with another R version; use the recorded version when reproducing the analysis.

:::

## uv: Python and its packages

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Create"}

Install uv once per computer by following
<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/>, then close and reopen the
terminal. Check that it works:

```{.bash}
uv --version
```

In your project folder, create the project file and choose a Python version:

```{.bash}
uv init --bare --python 3.13
uv python pin 3.13
```

`uv init --bare` writes `pyproject.toml`, which lists the packages your project asks
for, including a Python version requirement. Passing `--python 3.13` keeps that
requirement consistent with the version we choose. `uv python pin` writes
`.python-version`. If your computer does not have that
version of Python, uv downloads it the first time it is needed. Nothing is installed
yet; the environment appears when you run `uv sync`, `uv add`, or `uv run`.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Add packages"}

```{.bash}
uv add pandas jupyter
```

One command does three things: it adds the packages to `pyproject.toml`, records exact
versions in the lockfile `uv.lock`, and installs them into a new folder named `.venv`.
Add `jupyter` to any environment that will run Python chunks in Quarto.

```{.bash}
uv remove pandas
```

`uv remove` reverses all three. Unlike renv, there is no separate snapshot step; the
lockfile is updated every time.

| File or folder | Purpose | Share through Git? |
|---|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` | The packages you asked for. | Yes |
| `uv.lock` | The lockfile: every package's exact version. | Yes |
| `.python-version` | The Python version. | Yes |
| `.venv/` | The installed packages. | No; add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`. |

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Activate"}

You have two ways to use the environment from the terminal.

**Run one command inside it.** Put `uv run` in front. Nothing needs to be activated,
and uv first checks that the environment matches the lockfile:

```{.bash}
uv run python script.py
uv run quarto render
```

**Activate it for the whole terminal session.** After this, `python` and `quarto`
use the environment until you deactivate it or close the terminal:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## macOS and Linux

```{.bash}
source .venv/bin/activate
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```{.powershell}
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

:::

The terminal prompt then starts with the environment's name in parentheses.

**In Positron**, open the project folder. Positron looks for a `.venv` folder there
and lists it in the interpreter picker; choose it, and the Python console uses the
project's packages. This is separate from the terminal: choosing the interpreter does
not activate the environment for commands you type in the terminal.

**For Quarto**, render with `uv run quarto render`, or activate the environment first
and then run `quarto render`. Quarto can also discover a project `.venv`, but an
explicit Python setting or Jupyter kernel can affect which interpreter runs.
Check the interpreter path if the result is unexpected.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Deactivate"}

If you activated the environment in a terminal:

```{.bash}
deactivate
```

The prompt loses its prefix, and `python` means your computer's Python again. If you
only ever used `uv run`, there is nothing to deactivate.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Delete, and rebuild"}

The environment is the `.venv` folder. Delete it in Positron's file explorer, or from
the terminal:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## macOS and Linux

```{.bash}
rm -rf .venv
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```{.powershell}
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .venv
```

:::

Check the folder name before pressing Enter; these commands delete without asking.
Rebuild the environment from the lockfile at any time:

```{.bash}
uv sync --locked
```

A collaborator runs the same `uv sync --locked` after downloading your project. To stop using
uv in a project altogether, also delete `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and
`.python-version`.

:::

## pixi: one environment for Python, R, and more

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="What pixi is, and when to prefer it"}

pixi builds a single environment that can contain Python, R, their packages, and other
software such as command-line tools. Choose it when an analysis needs both languages
to share one environment, or needs software that renv and uv cannot install.

pixi installs packages from **conda-forge**, the community collection that conda also
draws on, but it is a separate program and you do not install conda. This has two
consequences worth knowing. R packages have an `r-` prefix, so dplyr is `r-dplyr`. And
conda-forge can lag behind: R itself and some R packages arrive there later than on
CRAN, and a few are not there at all.

Use renv **or** pixi for a project's R packages, not both.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Create"}

Install pixi once per computer by following <https://pixi.sh/latest/installation/>,
then close and reopen the terminal. In your project folder:

```{.bash}
pixi init
```

This writes `pixi.toml`, which lists what the project asks for, and a `.gitignore`
entry that keeps the installed packages out of Git. As with uv, the environment itself
appears when you add the first package.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Add packages"}

```{.bash}
pixi add python=3.13 pandas jupyter
pixi add r-base r-dplyr r-knitr r-rmarkdown
```

`python` and `r-base` are the languages themselves. `jupyter` lets Quarto run Python
chunks; `r-knitr` and `r-rmarkdown` let it run R chunks. Each `pixi add` updates
`pixi.toml`, records exact versions in the lockfile `pixi.lock`, and installs into a
hidden `.pixi` folder.

```{.bash}
pixi remove pandas
```

| File or folder | Purpose | Share through Git? |
|---|---|---|
| `pixi.toml` | The software you asked for. | Yes |
| `pixi.lock` | The lockfile: every package's exact version. | Yes |
| `.pixi/` | The installed software. | No; `pixi init` adds it to `.gitignore`. |

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Activate"}

The choices mirror uv's.

**Run one command inside the environment:**

```{.bash}
pixi run python script.py
pixi run Rscript analysis.R
pixi run quarto render
```

**Activate it for the terminal session:**

```{.bash}
pixi shell
```

`pixi shell` starts a new shell inside the current terminal with the environment
switched on. The command is the same on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

**In Positron**, open the project folder. Positron lists a pixi environment's Python
in the interpreter picker. Finding R inside a pixi environment is an experimental
Positron feature: switch on the setting `positron.r.interpreters.pixiDiscovery`, and
expect that some R features may not work as they do with an ordinary R installation.

**For Quarto**, render with `pixi run quarto render`.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Deactivate"}

Leave the shell that `pixi shell` started:

```{.bash}
exit
```

You are back in your ordinary terminal. If you only used `pixi run`, there is nothing
to deactivate.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Delete, and rebuild"}

```{.bash}
pixi clean
```

`pixi clean` removes the installed environment from the `.pixi` folder and keeps
`pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`. Rebuild it with:

```{.bash}
pixi install --locked
```

To stop using pixi in a project altogether, also delete `pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock`, and
the `.pixi` folder.

:::

## Check that Quarto uses your environment

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Ask the code where it is running"}

A rendered document can report which R or Python ran it. Put the chunk for your
language in a `.qmd` file in the practice folder and render it.

````{.markdown}
```{{r}}
R.version.string
.libPaths()[1]
```

```{{python}}
import sys
print(sys.version)
print(sys.prefix)
```
````

With renv, the library path should be inside the project's `renv/` folder. With uv,
`sys.prefix` should end in `.venv`. With pixi, it should end in `.pixi/envs/default`.

For R inside a pixi environment, check `R.home()` instead, which should be inside the
`.pixi` folder. `.libPaths()` can list a personal library first if your computer also
has an ordinary installation of the same R version, so pixi's R is less sealed off
from the rest of your computer than a renv project is.

If an R chunk fails with "The knitr package is not available", install knitr and
rmarkdown into the environment, as shown in the renv and pixi sections.

If a Python chunk fails, or reports a Python from somewhere else on your computer,
work through this list:

1. Did you render with `uv run quarto render` or `pixi run quarto render`, or activate
   the environment first?
2. Is `jupyter` installed in the environment? Quarto needs it to run Python chunks.
3. Does your computer have Jupyter kernels left over from other projects? Run
   `uv run jupyter kernelspec list` (or `pixi run jupyter kernelspec list`) to
   inspect them. The name `python3` does not by itself prove a kernel belongs to
   this project. For a Python-only document, select the Python kernel:

```{.yaml}
---
title: "My analysis"
jupyter: python3
---
```

Run `uv run quarto check jupyter` or `pixi run quarto check jupyter` to inspect
the Python environment Quarto sees, and verify `sys.prefix` in the rendered
document. A document containing both R and Python chunks normally uses knitr
and reticulate instead; see [Quarto's Python guide](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/python.html).

:::

## This book's environments

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Restore, do not create"}

The book's folder already contains its environments, so you restore them and do not
create new ones. Open the folder in Positron. For R, which every current chapter
uses, run this in the R console and agree when renv asks whether to install:

```{.r}
renv::restore()
```

For Python, which no current chapter needs yet, run this in the terminal:

```{.bash}
uv sync --locked
```

`--locked` tells uv to stop with an error if `uv.lock` is out of date, so it cannot
change the lockfile behind your back.

:::

## Good habits

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Small rules that prevent large problems"}

1. **One environment per project folder.** Do not share an environment between
   projects, and do not install a project's packages into your computer's general
   library.
2. **Commit the lockfile; ignore the installed packages.** `renv.lock`, `uv.lock`, and
   `pixi.lock` belong in Git. `renv/library`, `.venv`, and `.pixi` do not.
3. **Add packages with the tool.** Inside a uv project, use `uv add`, not
   `pip install`. Inside a pixi project, use `pixi add`. Otherwise the lockfile no
   longer describes what is installed.
4. **Record after you change.** With renv, run `renv::snapshot()` after adding or
   removing a package, and `renv::status()` when unsure.
5. **Report your versions.** When you write up results, state the versions of R or
   Python and of the main packages. The lockfile has them.

:::

## Practice

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Try it in a practice folder"}

1. Create an empty folder, open it in Positron, and set up renv. Install `jsonlite`,
   use it in a short `.R` file, and snapshot. Which line of `renv.lock` names
   jsonlite's version?
2. In the same folder, create a uv environment with `pandas`. Run
   `uv run python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"`. Then delete `.venv`
   and run the command again. What happens, and why?
3. A classmate sends you a project containing `renv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`, and
   `uv.lock`, with no `renv/library` or `.venv` folder. Which two commands set up
   both environments?
4. You ran `renv::install("survey")` and then `renv::snapshot()`, but `renv.lock`
   does not list survey. Name the likely reason.
5. Why does this book tell you to delete `.venv` freely but to think before running
   `renv::deactivate(clean = TRUE)`?

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Suggested answers"}

**1.** `renv.lock` has a `"jsonlite"` entry under `"Packages"`, and its `"Version"`
line holds the version.

**2.** The command works both times. `uv run` notices that the environment is missing
and rebuilds it from `uv.lock` before running Python. The lockfile, not the `.venv`
folder, is the record of the environment.

**3.** `renv::restore()` in the R console, and `uv sync` in the terminal.

**4.** No file in the project uses survey yet. The default snapshot records the
packages your code uses, so an installed but unused package is left out. Call the
package in a script or `.qmd` file, for example `survey::svydesign()`, and snapshot
again.

**5.** `.venv` holds only installed packages, which `uv sync` rebuilds from `uv.lock`.
`renv::deactivate(clean = TRUE)` deletes `renv.lock` as well, and without the lockfile
the exact versions cannot be rebuilt.

:::
